blocks.robotComment: TypeScript's whole superpower is catching bugs before you even hit run — let's see it in action. 🕵️
blocks.body: JavaScript never checks whether the values flowing through your code are the kind you expect until the moment that code actually runs. TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript, created by Microsoft, that layers a type system on top of it — so a whole category of mistakes gets caught the moment you save the file, before you ever hit run.

code.caption: In plain JavaScript, greet(42) would run and only crash later at name.toUpperCase() — numbers don't have that method. TypeScript catches the mistake immediately, right at the call site, before the code ever executes.

blocks.body: That's the core idea: TypeScript checks types at compile time — while you're writing the code — instead of at runtime, while it's running on someone's machine. The earlier a bug is caught, the cheaper and less embarrassing it is to fix.

blocks.robotComment: Autocomplete that actually knows what it's talking about — that's the payoff of typed code. 💡
blocks.body: Types also make your editor smarter. Once TypeScript knows a variable's exact shape, it can offer accurate autocomplete, flag typos in property names, and show you exactly what a function expects — all without running a single line of code.

code.code:
const user = { name: "Ravi", age: 29 };

user.ag; // Editor flags this immediately: Property 'ag' does not exist on type '{ name: string; age: number; }'. Did you mean 'age'?
code.caption: Because TypeScript knows user's exact shape, it catches the typo ag right away instead of silently returning undefined the way plain JavaScript would.

blocks.body: Here's the part that surprises a lot of beginners: browsers and Node.js can't run .ts files directly. TypeScript is compiled — translated — down into plain JavaScript before it ever runs. The type annotations only exist to help you while you write; by the time the code actually runs, they've been stripped away entirely.

blocks.sentence: TypeScript is a ___ of JavaScript that adds a type system on top of it.
blocks.explanation: TypeScript includes all of JavaScript and adds types on top — every valid JavaScript file is already close to valid TypeScript.

blocks.explanation: TypeScript analyzes your code and its types while you write, flagging mismatches immediately instead of waiting for them to surface as a crash later.

blocks.robotComment: Every language has an origin story — TypeScript's starts with one very experienced designer. 📜
blocks.body: TypeScript was created by Microsoft and first released in 2012, led by a programming-languages veteran named Anders Hejlsberg — the same person behind the C# language and, before that, Turbo Pascal and Delphi.

blocks.question: Which company created TypeScript?
blocks.explanation: TypeScript was created and is maintained by Microsoft, first released publicly in 2012.

blocks.body: The motivation was practical: as JavaScript codebases at Microsoft (and everywhere else) grew larger, plain JavaScript's lack of type checking made bugs harder to catch and large projects harder to maintain. TypeScript was designed specifically to add that missing safety net on top of JavaScript, without throwing away anything developers already knew.

blocks.sentence: TypeScript was designed by Microsoft to add ___ checking on top of the JavaScript developers already knew.
blocks.explanation: TypeScript's core purpose from the start was layering static type checking on top of existing JavaScript.

blocks.robotComment: Gradual adoption is basically TypeScript's superpower for winning over skeptical teams. 📈
blocks.body: That design choice — every valid JavaScript file being close to valid TypeScript — is exactly why adoption grew so fast. Teams could add TypeScript to an existing JavaScript project gradually, file by file, instead of rewriting everything from scratch.

Today, TypeScript is open source and widely used far beyond Microsoft — major frameworks and libraries across the JavaScript ecosystem either are written in TypeScript or ship with TypeScript type definitions for it.

blocks.robotComment: A colon and a type name — that's genuinely all it takes to lock a variable down. 🔒
blocks.body: A type annotation is how you tell TypeScript, up front, exactly what kind of value a variable is allowed to hold. You write it right after the variable name, separated by a colon.

code.code: let age: number = 29;
code.caption: : number is the annotation — it tells TypeScript that age must always hold a number, and nothing else.

blocks.body: Once a variable has a type, TypeScript holds it to that promise for the rest of its life. Try to assign a value of the wrong type later on, and TypeScript refuses — not while the program is running, but the moment you write the offending line.

code.code:
let age: number = 29;
age = "thirty"; // Error: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
code.caption: This is a compile error, caught before the code ever runs — nothing crashes in production because of it.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly the bug TypeScript exists to prevent — silent type drift. 🐛
blocks.body: Compare that to plain JavaScript, where the exact same reassignment would succeed silently. The bug — age suddenly being a string somewhere deep in the app — might not surface until much later, far from where it actually happened.

code.caption: JavaScript happily lets age become a string. Stopping exactly this kind of silent, hard-to-trace mistake is TypeScript's whole job.

blocks.robotComment: Three little words — string, number, boolean — and you've basically got JavaScript's whole value system covered. 🧩
blocks.body: TypeScript's most basic types map directly onto JavaScript's primitive values: string for text, number for all numbers, and boolean for true/false. Each one is written in lowercase, right after a variable's name.

code.caption: Each annotation matches the kind of value the variable is meant to hold — TypeScript will only ever allow that variable to be reassigned to a value of the same type.

blocks.robotComment: No int-vs-float headaches here — TypeScript keeps numbers refreshingly simple. 🔢
blocks.body: number covers every numeric value in TypeScript — whole numbers, decimals, negatives — there's no separate int, float, or double the way there is in some other languages. JavaScript only has one numeric type under the hood, and TypeScript matches that.

code.caption: Whole numbers, decimals, and negatives are all just number — TypeScript doesn't distinguish between them the way languages like Java or C# do.

blocks.body: string covers any text, written with single quotes, double quotes, or backticks for template literals — TypeScript doesn't care which quoting style you use, only that the value is text.

code.code:

let greeting: string = `Hello, ${city}!`;
code.caption: Both variables are typed string, whether the value was written with single quotes or built with a template literal.

blocks.explanation: TypeScript has a single number type for every numeric value, including decimals like 3.14 — there is no separate float type.

blocks.robotComment: Think back to how many numeric types you've actually seen so far. 🤔

blocks.robotComment: TypeScript is quietly smart about this — you often don't have to tell it anything at all. 🧠
blocks.body: You don't have to annotate every single variable. If you give a variable an initial value, TypeScript looks at that value and infers its type automatically — you get the same safety without typing it out yourself.

code.code:
let city = "Lagos"; // inferred as string, no annotation needed
city = 42; // Error: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.
code.caption: TypeScript never saw an explicit : string, but it inferred one from "Lagos" the moment the variable was declared — and it still enforces that type afterward.

blocks.body: This is why so much everyday TypeScript code looks just like plain JavaScript: as long as a variable is declared with an initial value, an explicit annotation would just be repeating information TypeScript already figured out on its own.

code.code:
let score = 100;      // inferred: number
let isDone = false;   // inferred: boolean
let label = "total";  // inferred: string
code.caption: None of these need annotations — the initial value already tells TypeScript everything it needs to know.

blocks.robotComment: This is the flip side of inference — no initial value means no free lunch. 🍽️
blocks.body: Inference stops working once there's no initial value to look at. Declare a variable without assigning it right away, and TypeScript can't guess what it's for — that's exactly when an explicit annotation earns its keep.

code.code:
let total;          // no initial value — inferred as 'any', losing type safety
let total2: number; // explicit annotation — TypeScript still enforces it once assigned

total2 = "oops"; // Error: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
code.caption: Without an annotation, total falls back to any and loses type checking entirely. total2 keeps its promise even though it wasn't assigned a value up front.

blocks.sentence: When a variable is declared with an initial value, TypeScript automatically ___ its type — no annotation required.
blocks.explanation: TypeScript reads the initial value and works out — infers — the matching type on its own, without you writing it explicitly.

options: When a variable is declared without an initial value

blocks.explanation: With no initial value to look at, TypeScript has nothing to infer from, so it falls back to any unless you annotate the variable explicitly.

blocks.robotComment: Inference is great until a function needs to know what's coming in — that's where you take over. ✍️
blocks.body: Inference works great for variables with an initial value, but it can't read your mind about function parameters — TypeScript has no way to know what a function is supposed to receive unless you tell it. That's where explicit annotations stop being optional and become essential.

code.caption: Each parameter gets its own : number annotation, and the : number written after the parentheses annotates the function's return value too.

blocks.robotComment: Skip the annotation and TypeScript just shrugs — any goes in, any comes out. 🤷

code.caption: The same [] pattern works for any type — string[] is an array of strings, boolean[] an array of booleans, and so on.

code.caption: scores is locked in as an array of numbers — TypeScript checks every element added to it afterward, not just the ones it started with.

blocks.body: That same idea works for any type — string[] for an array of strings, boolean[] for an array of booleans, even Product[] for an array of your own custom objects. blocks.robotComment: Fixed slots, fixed types — tuples are arrays with much stricter rules. 📌
blocks.body: A regular array like number[] can be any length, and every element shares the same type. A tuple is different: it's a fixed-length array where each position has its own, specific type. TypeScript checks both the length and the type at every position.

code.caption: The tuple type [string, number] describes exactly two slots: a string first, then a number. Not "an array of strings and numbers" — a specific pair in a specific order.

blocks.body: That ordering is the whole point of a tuple. Swap the values and TypeScript catches it immediately, the same way it would catch assigning a number where a string was expected. A plain string[] or number[] gives you no such guarantee about what lives at each index.

code.caption: Both the initial assignment and any later reassignment are checked against the position's declared type — position 0 is locked to string for the life of this tuple.

blocks.robotComment: Order matters here — swap two values and you've got a completely different meaning. 🔀
blocks.body: Tuples are a great fit whenever a fixed handful of related values travel together and their order carries meaning — a coordinate pair, an [error, result] pair from a function, or a [key, value] entry. Reading a tuple element gives you back the exact type declared for that position, not a generic union of every possible type in the tuple.

code.caption: Destructuring a tuple hands each variable the precise type from its position — result is known to be a number and status a string, not "number or string."

blocks.sentence: Unlike a regular array, a tuple has a fixed ___ and a specific type for each position.
blocks.explanation: A tuple type like [string, number] locks in exactly two slots — TypeScript checks both how many elements there are and what type belongs at each one.

blocks.question: Given let entry: [string, number] = ["score", 100];, what is the type of entry[1]?

blocks.robotComment: Same lockdown, now applied to a fixed-position tuple. 🧱

blocks.robotComment: any is TypeScript's overpowered escape hatch — great in a pinch, easy to abuse. ⚠️
blocks.body: Every TypeScript value has a type, but sometimes you need a variable that can hold literally anything and have TypeScript stay completely out of the way. That's what the any type is for — it's an escape hatch that opts a value out of type checking entirely.

code.code:
let value: any = 4;
value = "hello";   // fine, no error
value = true;      // fine, no error
value = [1, 2, 3]; // fine, no error
code.caption: A variable typed any accepts a reassignment to any other type, at any point, with no complaints from the compiler.

blocks.robotComment: This is the part that should make you a little nervous about any. 😬
blocks.body: The real danger of any isn't just that it accepts anything — it's that TypeScript stops checking what you do with it, too. Calling a method that doesn't exist, accessing a property that was never there, passing it somewhere it doesn't belong — all of that compiles without a single warning.

code.caption: With any, the mistake isn't caught while you're writing the code — it surfaces later, as a runtime crash, which is exactly what TypeScript exists to prevent.

blocks.body: Reaching for any every time a type is inconvenient to write defeats the entire purpose of using TypeScript — you get the extra syntax and the build step, but lose the safety net that's supposed to come with them. any has legitimate uses (gradually migrating old JavaScript, for example), but it should be the exception, not the default.

Nothing — unknown behaves exactly like a specific type already

questions.statement: A variable typed unknown can be assigned a string, then later a number, with no error.

questions.sentence: if (typeof value === "string") { value.toUpperCase(); } works because the typeof check ___ value from unknown to string.

questions.question: What values does the type "left" accept?
options: Only strings that start with the letter l

questions.statement: type Status = "on" | "off"; is an example of combining literal types with a union.

questions.sentence: function move(dir: "up" | "down") rejects a call like move("sideways") because "sideways" is not part of the ___.

questions.question: Compared to typing a parameter as plain string, a literal union like "left" | "right" mainly gives you:
options: Compile-time rejection of any value outside the allowed set
Automatic conversion of invalid values into valid ones
The ability to accept numbers as well
